question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
(x-6)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={(x-6)}^{2}{y}^{3/4}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-6>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined. Take $y>0$.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-6)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y={(x-6)}^{2}{y}^{3/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y}{(x-6)} & =(x-6){y}^{3/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={(x-6)}^{-1},\,q(x)=(x-6),\,n=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3/4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3/4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{(x-6)}^{-1}{y}^{1/4}=(x-6).\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-3/4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3/4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{(x-6)}^{-1}z=(x-6)
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-1}z=\frac{(x-6)}{4}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{4\cdot (x-6)},\,Q(x)=\frac{(x-6)}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (\frac{1}{4\cdot (x-6)})\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(1/4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-6)} \\  & ={(x-6)}^{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={(x-6)}^{1/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-1}z) & ={(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot (\frac{(x-6)}{4}) \\ {(x-6)}^{1/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{(x-6)}^{-3/4}z & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{(x-6)}^{1/4}) & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{(x-6)}^{1/4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{(x-6)}^{5/4}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{(x-6)}^{1/4} & =\frac{1}{9}{(x-6)}^{9/4}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=9{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/4}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{1/4}=\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}}\,⇒\,y={(\frac{{(x-6)}^{9/4}+C}{9{(x-6)}^{1/4}})}^{4}\,.
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above. Since $z=y^{1/4}>0$, retain only intervals where the displayed expression for $z$ is positive.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}+2\cdot (x-6)y}{{(x-6)}^{2}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-6>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}+2\cdot (x-6)y}{{(x-6)}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(x-6)}^{2}}+\frac{2\cdot (x-6)y}{{(x-6)}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2{(x-6)}^{-1}y & ={(x-6)}^{-2}{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-2{(x-6)}^{-1},\,q(x)={(x-6)}^{-2},\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-2{(x-6)}^{-1}{y}^{-1}={(x-6)}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2{(x-6)}^{-1}z={(x-6)}^{-2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2{(x-6)}^{-1}z=-{(x-6)}^{-2}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{(x-6)},\,Q(x)=-\frac{1}{{(x-6)}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/(x-6))\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-6)} \\  & ={(x-6)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={(x-6)}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2{(x-6)}^{-1}z) & ={(x-6)}^{2}\cdot (-{(x-6)}^{-2}) \\ {(x-6)}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2\cdot (x-6)z & =-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({(x-6)}^{2}z) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({(x-6)}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =-\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ {(x-6)}^{2}z & =-(x-6)+C \\ z & =\frac{C-(x-6)}{{(x-6)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-(x-6)}{{(x-6)}^{2}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{{(x-6)}^{2}}{C-(x-6)}\,.
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
{(x-6)}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}-(x-6)y.
$$

Work on an interval where $x-6>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which all displayed real expressions are defined. Take $y>0$.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{-1/2}-(x-6)y \\ {(x-6)}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+(x-6)y & ={y}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{(x-6)}^{-1}y & ={(x-6)}^{-2}{y}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={(x-6)}^{-1},\,q(x)={(x-6)}^{-2},\,n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we multiply the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+{(x-6)}^{-1}{y}^{3/2}={(x-6)}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{(x-6)}^{-1}z={(x-6)}^{-2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-1}z=\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-2}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{3}{2\cdot (x-6)},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{2{(x-6)}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (\frac{3}{2\cdot (x-6)})\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(3/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-6)} \\  & ={(x-6)}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={(x-6)}^{3/2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{3/2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-1}z) & ={(x-6)}^{3/2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-2}) \\ {(x-6)}^{3/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{1/2}z & =\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({(x-6)}^{3/2}z) & =\frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({(x-6)}^{3/2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{2}{(x-6)}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ {(x-6)}^{3/2}z & =3{(x-6)}^{1/2}+C \\ z & =\frac{3\sqrt{(x-6)}+C}{{(x-6)}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3/2}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{3/2}=\frac{3\sqrt{(x-6)}+C}{{(x-6)}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{{(3\sqrt{(x-6)}+C)}^{2/3}}{(x-6)}\,.
$$

First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-6)}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={(x-6)}^{3}{y}^{2}+(x-6)y \\ {(x-6)}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-(x-6)y & ={(x-6)}^{3}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{(x-6)} & =(x-6){y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{(x-6)},\,q(x)=(x-6),\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{{y}^{-1}}{(x-6)}=(x-6).\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x-6)}z=(x-6)
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{(x-6)}z=-(x-6)
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{(x-6)},\,Q(x)=-(x-6)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/(x-6))\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-6)} \\  & =(x-6)\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=(x-6)$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-6)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{(x-6)}z) & =(x-6)\cdot (-(x-6)) \\ (x-6)\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-{(x-6)}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x-6)z) & =-{(x-6)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x-6)z)\,\text{d}x & =-\int {(x-6)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ (x-6)z & =-\frac{{(x-6)}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{(x-6)}^{3}}{3\cdot (x-6)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{(x-6)}^{3}}{3\cdot (x-6)}\,⇒\,y=\frac{3\cdot (x-6)}{C-{(x-6)}^{3}}\,.
$$

These are the nonzero real solutions on the specified intervals; exclude denominator zeros and restrict constants and intervals to the real branches used above.

$$
{(x+6)}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(x+6)}^{3}{y}^{2}+(x+6)y.
